query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine‐learning interatomic potential (ML-IAP) rigorously trained on high-temperature, multicomponent ab initio data will improve the reference–target phase-space overlap for HEAs, thereby reducing the thermodynamic integration (TI) path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in both the solid and liquid states at conditions near their high melting temperatures, exhibiting a wide diversity of atomic configurations.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a machine-learning interatomic potential (e.g., a neural network or moment tensor potential) that is trained on high-fidelity ab initio data capturing the high-temperature liquid-phase configurations of HEAs.
generation.conditions: Applicable to HEAs with near-equiatomic compositions, for simulations performed at or near the melting point (high-temperature regime) where both solid and liquid phases are relevant.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML-IAP acts as the intermediary that better represents the complete distribution of atomic configurations in the ab initio liquid, thereby bridging the gap between the simplified EAM representation and the true system behavior.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating a training set enriched in high-temperature liquid-phase configurations, the ML model better captures the complex, many-body interactions present in the HEA, leading to improved phase-space overlap between the reference (ML-IAP) and target (ab initio) potentials. This enhanced overlap should reduce the thermodynamic integration path mismatch compared to what is achieved using TOR-TILD’s EAM references.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable decrease in the TI path mismatch—potentially in the range of a 20-30% reduction relative to EAM-based methods—resulting in more reliable free energy computations for both the solid and liquid phases.
generation.baseline: Current TOR-TILD implementations using EAM references, which inadequately capture the diversity of atomic configurations in the ab initio liquid phase, resulting in a larger TI path mismatch.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only in high-entropy alloys under high-temperature conditions near melting; the method’s efficacy outside this regime (e.g., for off-equiatomic compositions or lower temperatures) remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the TI path mismatch reduction is uncertain and likely to vary with alloy composition, the quality of the ab initio training data, and temperature; further benchmarking against experimental or high-level computational free energies is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform free energy calculations on a selected multicomponent HEA system at near-melting conditions using two approaches: one with the traditional TOR-TILD EAM reference and another employing the newly developed ML-IAP. Evaluate phase-space overlap and TI path mismatch using both methods.
measurements: Quantitative phase-space overlap metrics (e.g., overlap integrals between reference and target probability distributions)
Thermodynamic integration path mismatch (e.g., differences in free energy integration paths)
Computed free energy differences compared to high-fidelity ab initio benchmarks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-IAP does not reduce the TI path mismatch by a significant margin (e.g., less than a ~10% improvement compared to the TOR-TILD EAM reference) or if the free energy estimates do not converge closer to ab initio benchmarks, then the hypothesis is falsified.

frame.goal: To develop a single, testable methodological intervention that improves the phase-space overlap between the reference and target systems during thermodynamic integration, thereby reducing the integration path mismatch compared to existing TOR-TILD methods using EAM references.
frame.limitation: EAM references currently fail to adequately represent the many atomic configurations present in the ab initio liquid phase, limiting the accuracy of thermodynamic-integrations in these multicomponent systems near melting temperatures.
root_cause_cues: inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid
thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references
constraints: The intervention must be single and testable.
It should apply to both solid and liquid phases.
It must operate at or near high melting temperatures.
It must quantitatively predict the reduction in TI path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references.
The applicable composition and temperature ranges need to be defined.
Support must be drawn from evidence in elemental or binary calculations.
A decisive free-energy benchmark must be identified that could falsify the proposed hypothesis.
frame.regime: High-temperature conditions at or near the melting point of HEAs, encompassing both the solid and liquid phases.
prior_attempts: TOR-TILD’s use of EAM references, which has been shown to have insufficient phase-space overlap due to a limited ability to capture the diverse atomic configurations in ab initio liquids.

families.principle: Utilize machine learning to develop interatomic potentials that capture the full complexity and diversity of atomic configurations present in the ab initio liquid; these models can be trained on high-fidelity ab initio data to yield improved representation and phase-space overlap.
